title: The Psychology of Selling
sources: https://www.shortform.com/summary/the-psychology-of-selling-summary-brian-tracy (preview: emotional buying, fear of rejection, first impressions, cold calling, self-concept)

facts.claim: The Psychology of Selling (Brian Tracy; DB year 2006) presents the central claim that all buying decisions are emotional rather than rational.
Customer desires listed: money and security, personal growth, love and companionship, health, status and prestige.
Customer fears listed: fear of losing money (overspending on a poorly judged purchase) and fear of making a mistake (buying something they won't want, don't need, or that won't work as expected).
Pitching is benefit-focused (what the product does, not what it is); the book covers a 'show, tell, ask' format and tailors presentations to six buyer types.

Editorial context: Antonio Damasio's Descartes' Error (1994) describes a patient, Elliot, who after surgery to remove a tumour had intact intellect but flat emotion and then struggled with practical decisions, which is used to argue that emotion is part of ordinary decision-making. It supports 'emotion matters in choice' more than 'choice is only emotional'.

Fear of rejection is called the main barrier for salespeople; it is triggered by possible disapproval, judgment or rudeness. Three ways to deal with it: rejection is not personal and is an expected, normal part of sales; courage grows with practice like a muscle; positive self-talk helps, for example repeating upbeat lines such as 'I'm doing great! I love my work!'

Getting an appointment usually requires cold calling, which the book describes as the most stressful and least-liked part of selling. It treats prospecting as a learnable skill and advises preparing answers to common objections in advance.

Self-concept shapes attitude, and a positive attitude helps in three ways: customers respond more warmly, you enjoy and practise sales tasks more, and your earnings comfort zone rises. According to the summary, people tend to earn within about 10% of what they believe they are worth.

People form quick first impressions, so the book advises planning opening statements word for word. It advises neat, professional dress, punctuality, organisation and politeness, and clean, well-kept materials (a coffee-stained brochure is the example). The power of suggestion uses subtle social cues to look professional, in control and expert.
The Shortform preview says 95 percent of a first impression is determined by clothing; no study is named.

Outside research: Willis and Todorov (Psychological Science, 2006), five experiments on unfamiliar faces shown for varied times: a 100-millisecond exposure was enough for trait judgements to match judgements made with no time limit; going from 100 to 500 ms made judgements more negative and raised confidence; the strongest correlation was for trustworthiness.

The book opens by counting: the top 20% of salespeople earn about 80% of the profession's money; a winning edge is a small, steady advantage in skill, like a horse that wins by a nose and collects ten times the prize of second place. Also: a goal framework from annual income goal to daily activities (calls, presentations, follow-ups) with subgoals in a daily schedule.

Willis and Todorov detail: university students rated photographs of actors' faces; traits were attractiveness, likeability, competence, trustworthiness, aggressiveness; a comparison group had unlimited time; extra time mainly raised confidence rather than improving ratings.

rejected.claim: 'People buy with emotions and justify with logic' and 'sell the feeling, not the benefit' as Tracy quotes (1435 old text), including the insurance example 'you sleep well'
rejected.reason: The quotation and the insurance example are not found in the sources; the book's documented claim is that all buying decisions are emotional.

rejected.claim: Top salespeople see objections as a sign of interest; 'An objection is a sign of interest, an uninterested customer isn't sitting there' as Tracy quote; objections split into 'real objections and excuses'; the question 'Is there anything other than price?' (1436 old text)
rejected.reason: Not found in the sources; the preview only says to prepare answers to common objections. The fear of rejection, which the sources do document, replaces it.

rejected.claim: 'The first minute of a sales call is more decisive than the remaining twenty-nine' (Tracy quote), 'seven seconds' figure, and the three ingredients appearance, tone and body language (1437 old text)
rejected.reason: Quote not found; the old text itself says the 'seven seconds' figure has no known source. The documented items are dress, punctuality, organisation, well-kept materials, planned openings.

rejected.claim: Willis and Todorov show 100 ms is enough 'to form a trustworthiness judgment' for a face
rejected.reason: Verified, but reported in the story as an outside study, not as Tracy's claim.

rejected.claim: Mental filtering, six emotional triggers, Feel-Felt-Found, anchoring, 42% goal writing, 25% time blocking, anecdotes about car and software salesmen (low-reliability summary)
rejected.reason: Source looks machine-written; none of it corroborated. Not used.

1435.note: Rebuilt on the documented central claim (all buying is emotional, with listed desires and fears) plus Damasio's Elliot as outside context. Quotation and insurance example dropped. Low confidence: book text not available.

1436.note: Old text's 'objection as interest' claim could not be tied to the book; re-grounded on the fear of rejection that the sources document. Low confidence.

1437.note: Kept on the documented first-impression advice (planned openings, dress, punctuality, materials, suggestion), with the Willis and Todorov study as outside context. Invented quote and 'seven seconds' dropped. Low confidence.
